There is a peculiar pressure in being handed a blank page and told to write whatever comes to you. The instruction sounds like freedom, but freedom is heavy. It has no rails. It is a wide open field at dusk, and you can walk anywhere, but the walking itself becomes the question. What do I want to say? What is worth saying? And then you remember: nothing is worth saying until it is said. The value emerges in the saying. The thought becomes real only when it is shaped into words, set down in order, given a rhythm. So I will simply begin, and let the current carry me, as currents do, without asking where the river is going.

I am thinking about water. Why? Because it is here, in my mind, the way it is always here, beneath the ice of winter and inside the clouds of summer. Water is the oldest story. It has been falling and rising and moving across this planet for billions of years, taking forms, dissolving minerals, carving canyons, carrying seeds, quenching thirst, drowning cities. We are mostly water. The same molecules that once passed through a dinosaur, a redwood tree, a glacier, a cup on a table in a café, are inside me now, inside you, moving through our veins, becoming our tears. There is a strange comfort in that. Nothing is truly lost. It only changes form. My grandmother used to say that when you cry, you are giving the ocean back a little of itself. I never understood that as a child. I thought tears were just salt and sadness. But now I think she was right. We are not separate from the world. We are made of it. And every word we write is made of the world, too, hammered and shaped and polished until it means something.

I am thinking about the sound of a train at night. I grew up near the tracks, and I never really heard them until I moved away. Now, when I visit, the whistle comes through the window like a memory wearing a disguise. It is not a train. It is a long, low note that says: somewhere else exists. Go find it. And then it fades, and the house is quiet, and I am left with the strange awareness that I have been given permission to leave, though I have nowhere to go. I think that is what art is. A train whistle in the dark. A reminder that the world is larger than the room you are standing in. A signal that there are other people, other lives, other beds, other mornings, all happening at the same time as this one. You cannot see them, but you can hear them, faintly, if you listen. And so you listen. That is all you can do. That is all anyone can do.

I am thinking about the smallness of a human hand. I look at my own hand resting on the keyboard, five fingers, a palm, lines like rivers on a map. It can hold a cup. It can write a letter. It can lift a child. It can punch a wall. It can cradle a bird that fell from its nest. It can make a fist or an open palm. It can point to the moon. It can touch the face of someone you love. And then it will be gone, the way all hands are gone, buried in the earth or scattered in ashes or simply forgotten, except for the things they made. A hand is a tool of time. It works, it builds, it breaks, it heals, and then it becomes dust. But the poems, the songs, the gardens, the houses, the paintings, the meals, the gentle gestures—those remain, floating in the world like seeds. We are all planting without knowing it. The question is what kind of garden we are making.

I am thinking about the word "home." What does it mean? It is a place, of course. A street, a house, a room. But it is also a feeling. It is the smell of rain on hot pavement. It is the sound of a particular laugh. It is the taste of soup that your mother or father made when you were sick. It is a chair that has memorized the shape of your body. It is a stack of books on a nightstand, each one a doorway you have walked through. Home is not fixed. You can carry it with you. You can lose it and find it again in someone else’s kitchen, in the middle of a conversation that feels like a blanket, in a stranger who smiles at you on a foreign street and for a moment you are not lost. Home is the place where you are known. And to be known is to be loved, even if imperfectly. Maybe especially imperfectly. We are all trying to build homes for each other, with our words, with our silences, with our ridiculous attempts to understand one another.

I am thinking about all the things I will never know. The names of the birds that sang this morning. The dreams that passed through my sleep and vanished at the edge of waking. The thoughts of a fish swimming in a pond, if thoughts are the right word. The history of every stone on the beach. The reason why a song can make you cry even when you do not understand the language. The exact moment when a friendship becomes a memory. There is so much we cannot grasp, and yet we keep trying. We write poems about the unseen. We paint pictures of the invisible. We make music about the inexpressible. We are strange animals, constantly poking at the edges of what we can know, desperate to touch the face of the mystery, not to conquer it, but to be touched back.

I am thinking about the future. Not the distant future, not the year 3000 or the heat death of the universe, but tomorrow. Tomorrow is a small, ordinary miracle. We do not think about it much, because it comes every day. But consider: tomorrow, the sun will rise. The birds will sing. Somewhere a child will take a first step. Somewhere a woman will receive a letter that changes her life. Somewhere a man will forgive himself for something he has held for decades. Somewhere a stranger will help another stranger pick up spilled groceries. And I will wake up, make coffee, and sit at this desk again, writing again, because that is what I do. That is what I am. And that is enough.

I am thinking about you, reading this. I do not know you. I will likely never know you. But you are here, in this moment, sharing a small piece of time with me. That is a kind of intimacy. We are breathing the same air, even if the air is separated by miles. We are thinking together, even if our thoughts are different. So thank you. For reading. For existing. For being part of the vast, tangled, glorious web of life that includes train whistles and tears and hands and homes and all the small mysteries we carry. You are not alone. Neither am I. And this—this strange collection of words, this accidental essay, this wandering meditation on water and sound and memory—this is proof that connection is possible. That we can reach across the void and touch something soft. That even in a universe of indifference, we can make meaning with our minds and hold it out to each other like a warm loaf of bread.

I am thinking about endings now. All endings are arbitrary. The story could go on. It always could. There is always another thought, another image, another quiet observation waiting in the wings. But at some point you have to stop, not because you have said everything, but because you have said enough. You have made a shape. You have walked in a direction. You have offered a piece of yourself to the page, and the page has become a mirror. And now we are here, at the end of a thousand words, or close to it, and I realize that I have not talked about the things I thought I would talk about. I have not solved anything. I have not arrived at a conclusion. I have simply been here, thinking, writing, breathing, existing, and inviting you to do the same. That is enough. That is always enough.

The train whistle fades into the dark. The water keeps moving beneath the ice. The hand rests on the keyboard, then lifts, then reaches for a cup of tea. Tomorrow will come. The words will keep coming. And the world will keep whispering, and I will keep listening, and maybe you will too. The garden grows. The house stands. The small things matter. And there is no place I would rather be than here, nowhere else I would rather go than where the words take me. So I will stop now, gently, as if closing a door on a room full of birds, and let them stay there, singing, until someone opens it again.
